transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. Can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Um, well, I guess... I mean, what really brought me in, what finally made me make the appointment and actually show up today, is that my mind just won't stay on one thing anymore. It’s like I have a dozen different radio stations playing in my head all at once, and someone keeps changing the channel every two seconds. I work as a jeweler, right? I make and repair custom pieces, which takes an incredible amount of focus. You have to be precise down to the millimeter. But lately, I’ll be sitting at my bench, and I’ll start reading a customer email about a ring sizing, and then before I even finish the sentence, I’m looking at a saw mark on a piece of scrap metal from three days ago, wondering if I should buff it out. And then a car drives by outside, or I hear a dog bark, and suddenly I’m thinking about that, and then I look down and realize I’ve completely lost the whole work order I was supposed to be doing. I’ll spend twenty minutes looking for a tiny diamond I thought I dropped, only to realize I never even took it out of the safe. It’s just... it’s exhausting, honestly. I can’t seem to hold a single thought in my head long enough to finish anything.
Have you always had trouble staying focused like this, even back in school or childhood, or is this a new change from how your mind used to work?

No, no, it was never like this. I mean, back in high school... well, high school was high school, you know? I wasn't exactly the valedictorian or anything, I wasn't sitting there reading giant history textbooks for fun, but I could pay attention. Especially when it mattered. Like in my shop classes. That's actually where I first got into metalwork, back in eleventh grade. I had this teacher, Mr. Henderson, and he gave us this assignment to make a copper box from scratch. You had to measure it out, score it, cut it, solder the joints... and I would just sit there for the whole hour-and-a-half block period, completely zoned in. I wouldn't even hear the bell ring at the end of the day. I was just so focused on getting the solder to flow perfectly along the seam, making sure it was completely flush. 

So, no, I definitely had focus. I mean, sure, maybe I'd daydream a little in math class if the teacher was droning on, but who doesn't? But this thing that's happening right now... this is completely different. It's not just being a little bored or distracted. It’s like a switch flipped recently. I used to be able to sit at my jeweler's bench for four, five hours straight, just me and the metal and the torch, just totally in the zone, and now... now I can't even get through a three-minute email without getting up to check the window, or looking at my phone, or starting to polish a pendant that doesn't even need polishing yet. So yeah, it's definitely a new change. It's really not how my brain is supposed to work at all.
Along with this trouble focusing, have you noticed any changes in your mood—like feeling unusually sad, hopeless, or low, or on the other hand, unusually energetic, elated, or 'wired'?

Well, yeah... actually, yes. It's funny you ask about feeling sad or low because it's been really bad lately. It's not the wired feeling, not right now anyway. Right now, it's just... heavy. Like, these past couple of weeks, I've been waking up, and before my feet even hit the floor, I just have this intense, hollow feeling right in the center of my chest. It's like the shine has completely gone out of everything. And I mean everything. I used to love the mornings, getting to the shop early, turning on the lights, seeing all the tools laid out, but lately... lately I just sit in my truck in the parking lot. 

Just the other day, I was sitting there with the engine off, staring at the front door of the shop, and I just started crying. For no reason! I just sat there with tears running down my face, feeling so incredibly hopeless and empty, and I couldn't even bring myself to put the key in the lock for almost forty-five minutes. And it's not just a passing thing, it's this constant, dragging weight. It makes everything feel pointless. Even when I'm trying to work, trying to get through those emails or fix a clasp, I just feel so drained and sad, like I'm moving through molasses. It's just this dark cloud that won't lift, no matter what I do or how much I try to just push through it. So, yeah, definitely feeling unusually sad and low. It's really taking a toll on me.

Before these past two weeks of low mood started, have you ever had a period—lasting several days or more—where you felt unusually elevated, euphoric, or irritable, needed much less sleep than usual but still felt full of energy, or found yourself talking faster or taking on more risks than normal?

Well, actually, yeah. It’s funny you ask that because right before this whole heavy, dark cloud thing started, I had this... this stretch of time where I was just on fire. Not literally, obviously, but man, I felt incredible. It was right after I did this local artisan craft show downtown. Usually, those things are exhausting, you know? You’re standing on concrete all weekend, talking to a hundred people a day, packing and unpacking inventory. But this time, after the show ended on Sunday night, I didn't feel tired at all. I felt... lit up. Just absolutely electric and, I don't know, larger than life. 

I remember driving back to the shop that night, and it was like I could see everything so clearly, like I had all the answers to everything I’d ever wanted to do with my business. I was buzzing. And it didn't stop on Sunday. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday... I was just riding this massive wave. I felt like I was ten feet tall and could take on the world. But the weird thing was, it wasn't just feeling good. I was also getting really, really irritated with people. Like, I’d be in the shop, feeling like a genius because I had this brilliant new idea for a line of silver cuffs, and my assistant or even some of my regular customers would come in and ask me something totally normal, like if I was going to stick to the regular shop hours that week. And I would just snap. 

I mean, I completely bit my assistant's head off on a Thursday because she told me I needed to slow down and maybe go home and get some rest. I was like, "Why would I sleep? I'm creating masterpieces here! You're just trying to hold me back!" It was so out of character for me to talk to her like that, but in the moment, I just felt so superior, so elevated above all the mundane, boring stuff everyone else was worried about. One minute I was on top of the world, feeling euphoric, and the next I was just furious that everyone else was moving in slow motion and trying to drag me down to their level. So yeah, I definitely had a period like that right before I crashed into this awful depression.
How many days in a row did that intense, high-energy, irritable period last before your mood shifted into this depression?

Well, let me think... so the show ended on that Sunday night, and actually, that's when they announced the awards for the different artisan categories. I had submitted this really intricate sterling silver collar piece I'd been working on for months, and I actually won first place in the metalwork division, which was just... I mean, that was part of why I was feeling so incredibly validated and on top of the world. So that was Sunday. And then Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday... it just kept going. 

I remember the following weekend, I was still completely wired. I was in the shop at 3:00 AM on a Saturday, blasting music, hammering out these new designs, completely losing track of time. And it just... it didn't stop. It wasn't just a few days. That whole out-of-control, electric, snappy stretch... it went on for about two solid weeks. Two weeks of just barely sleeping, running on pure adrenaline and whatever that feeling was, just churning out work and getting mad at anyone who got in my way. It was a full fourteen days, maybe even a little more, before it finally started to fizzle out and I crashed into this... this heavy, dark place I'm in now. But yeah, it was about two weeks straight of just being completely wired.
During these past two weeks of feeling so low and hopeless, have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself or that you'd be better off dead?

Well... yeah. It's really hard to admit that out loud, but... yes. When I'm sitting in my truck, like I was telling you about, or when I finally drag myself inside the shop and just stare at my workbench doing absolutely nothing... my mind just goes to these really, really dark places. I start thinking about my family, you know? They see me struggling like this, just completely useless, and I know it weighs heavily on them. And my clients, too. I've got people waiting on custom pieces—engagement rings, anniversary gifts, things that are really important to them—and I'm just letting everyone down right now. I can't even bring myself to answer their calls or reply to an email. 

So I just keep having these thoughts... it's like this constant drumbeat in my head telling me that my family, and my clients, and just everyone in my life would honestly be better off if I wasn't around anymore. Like, if I just wasn't here to be this massive burden and disappointment to them, their lives would be so much easier. And, I mean, I want to be clear, I don't have a plan. I'm not sitting there trying to figure out how to actually do it or anything like that. I haven't thought about a specific way to end things or hurt myself. 

But... man, it just really scares me. It scares me how often the thought comes up. It's like a tape loop playing in the background all day long. I'll just be holding a piece of silver, or holding a polishing cloth, staring at the wall, and my brain just casually tells me they wouldn't have to deal with my mess if I were gone. It happens so much lately, multiple times a day, and it's just terrifying to feel like your own brain is turning against you like that, especially when I don't even have the energy to fight it off.
